title: Assignment 3: Anatomy of a Chart
text:
2. Anscombe’s Quartet
The four Anscombe datasets have nearly identical regression statistics, but their plots show very different patterns.


Code
data(anscombe)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot_colors <- c(
  "steelblue",
  "firebrick",
  "darkgreen",
  "purple"
)

plot_symbols <- c(
  16,
  17,
  15,
  18
)

line_types <- c(
  1,
  2,
  3,
  4
)

for(i in 1:4) {

  x <- anscombe[[paste0("x", i)]]
  y <- anscombe[[paste0("y", i)]]

  plot(
    x,
    y,
    main = paste("Dataset", i),
    xlab = paste0("x", i),
    ylab = paste0("y", i),
    pch = plot_symbols[i],
    col = plot_colors[i]
  )

  abline(
    lm(y ~ x),
    col = plot_colors[i],
    lty = line_types[i],
    lwd = 2
  )
}









Code
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))



Regression Comparison


Code
results <- data.frame(
  Dataset = 1:4,
  Intercept = NA,
  Slope = NA,
  R_squared = NA,
  Residual_SE = NA
)

for(i in 1:4) {

  x <- anscombe[[paste0("x", i)]]
  y <- anscombe[[paste0("y", i)]]

  model <- lm(y ~ x)

  results$Intercept[i] <- coef(model)[1]
  results$Slope[i] <- coef(model)[2]
  results$R_squared[i] <- summary(model)$r.squared
  results$Residual_SE[i] <- summary(model)$sigma
}

results

Although the four datasets have nearly identical slopes, intercepts, R-squared values, and residual standard errors, the visual patterns are very different. Summary statistics alone can hide nonlinear relationships, outliers, and unusual data structures that become clear when the data are plotted.

text:
4. Reproduce the Tuned Chart with ggplot2


Code
library(ggplot2)

anscombe1 <- data.frame(
  x = anscombe$x1,
  y = anscombe$y1
)

ggplot(
  anscombe1,
  aes(x = x, y = y)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "steelblue",
    shape = 17,
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "firebrick",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Anscombe Dataset 1",
    x = "x1",
    y = "y1"
  ) +
  theme_classic(
    base_family = "serif"
  )









The serif font became a theme() setting through theme_classic(base_family = "serif"). The fixed point colour, shape, and size were specified directly in geom_point() rather than through scale_*() functions because they were not mapped to data variables. Therefore, none of the settings in this particular chart required a scale_*() function. The regression line added with abline() in base R was reproduced with geom_smooth(method = "lm"). All of the tuned base-R settings used here had a practical ggplot2 equivalent.

title: Assignment 1
text: Anscombe’s four datasets may have similar statistical results, but the actual data patterns identified by graphs are very different. The first dataset shows a relatively normal linear relationship, but the second dataset shows a curved pattern. So, a simple linear regression line does not fully explain the data pattern. In the third dataset, most of the points show a consistent pattern, but one outlier strongly influences the result. Lastly, in the fourth dataset, most points are concentrated in one location, but one point strongly impacts the result. Anscombe’s four datasets show that it is difficult to fully understand the actual data pattern by just checking the mean, correlation, and regression results. Therefore, when we analyze data, it is suggested to draw graphs first and check the patterns and outliers instead of just checking the statistical results.

3. Crime Rate Chart Critique

This graph shows the trend in Index crime in the United States from 2014 to 2024, and it is good to see the changes in the overall crime rate by separating violent crime and property crime. Also, it has a good point that the graph clearly indicates that the 2021 data are not comparable with other years. However, there is also a critical point: the 2024 data are not final annual data but preliminary data estimated based on the percent change between 2023 and early 2024, but they are described in almost the same way as other years’ final data. In other words, readers can misunderstand that the 2024 data are also final data like other years. Also, the title indicates that the crime rate in 2024 is the lowest since 1961, but the graph only shows crime rates from 2014 to 2024, so the readers cannot check the long-term comparison themselves through the graph. Lastly, the total height of the bar already shows the total Index crime, but showing the same value again with a line may be redundant. Therefore, the 2024 estimated numbers should be clearly distinguished using a different color or separate annotation. Also, to support the title of long-term comparison, data from a longer time period should be presented to increase the accuracy and clarity of the graph.
Source: Prison Policy Initiative, “U.S. crime rates continue to fall, and preliminary data indicate that the 2024 crime rate was the lowest since 1961”

I used the 2024 ACS 5-year estimates for Texas counties. I used median household income (B19013_001) for the map and calculated the poverty rate using the number of people below poverty (B17001_002) divided by the poverty universe (B17001_001). I also kept the margins of error because ACS estimates include sampling uncertainty. The poverty-rate margin of error was calculated using moe_prop(). The results show that county rankings should be interpreted carefully because counties with similar estimates may have overlapping confidence intervals.

Website Results
The five-year file covered September 2021 to September 2026, and the data were monthly. When I changed the time window to one year, the data changed to weekly.
Google Trends does not show actual search counts. The values are scaled from 0 to 100. A value of 100 represents the peak level of relative search interest within the query, while 0 represents very low relative interest.
I also removed “Election” from the original query and downloaded the data again. The values for Trump and Kamala Harris changed. This showed that the values are rescaled depending on which search terms are included in the query.

title: Assignment 2
text:
Google Trends in R
I also collected Google Trends data using the gtrendsR package in R. The R object contained more information than the website CSV. It included interest by country, region, DMA, and city, as well as related topics and related queries.

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

the_df <- TrumpHarrisElection$interest_over_time

write_csv(
  the_df,
  paste0("gtrends_us_5y_", Sys.Date(), ".csv")
)


library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

cached_data <- read_csv(
  "gtrends_us_5y_2026-09-09.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

cached_data$hits_num <- parse_number(cached_data$hits)

ggplot(cached_data,
       aes(x = date, y = hits_num, color = keyword)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Google Trends Interest Over Time",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Search interest",
    color = "Search term"
  )








I compared “Kamala Harris” and “Harris,” and the two series were not the same. “Harris” is a broader search term and can include searches that are not about Kamala Harris. This showed that the search term used can affect what is actually being measured.

title: Assignment 2
text:
Comparing the Two Methods
The website and R results were not exactly the same. For example, for September 2021, the website value for Trump was 4, while the R-based value was 1, which was 3 points lower.
The R method was easier to reproduce because the search settings were written directly in the code. It would also be easier to use R if I needed to collect data for many search terms. With the website method, I had to record the search settings manually.
Both methods can also have problems. The website interface can change, while gtrendsR depends on an unofficial service and may be affected by rate limits or changes to Google Trends.
I ran the same gtrendsR call twice a few minutes apart. In my run, the two results were identical. However, Google Trends uses sampled search data, so repeated pulls are not guaranteed to always return the same values.

When Is Scraping the Right Tool?
Web scraping is appropriate when the information needed for research is publicly available on a website but is not available through a structured API, downloadable dataset, or other reliable machine-readable source. When an official API or structured dataset exists, it is generally preferable because its schema and data-generation process are more stable and reproducible than scraping a changing webpage.

4. Data Plan

Web Data Acquisition Plan
For my research, I am interested in crime analysis, policing, public safety, environmental criminology, crime mapping, and GIS. One potential source is the City of Dallas Open Data and Police Public Data system, which provides public access to police offense and incident information. I would prefer this official source because the data are published by the City of Dallas and Dallas Police Department and are more appropriate for analyzing local crime patterns and locations than a third-party website.
Before collecting data, I would check the applicable robots.txt file for the specific endpoint and comply with any restrictions it specifies. The City of Dallas makes public data available for exploration and analysis through its Open Data system, while its general website disclaimer restricts commercial use without written permission. The City also provides structured access through GIS REST services, including police geographic layers that support formats such as JSON and GeoJSON and pagination. Therefore, when the necessary variables are available through an API, REST service, or downloadable dataset, I would use those structured sources rather than scrape webpages directly. Web scraping would only be used when relevant public information is available on a webpage but not through a structured alternative.
For a project examining crime patterns and neighborhood change, I would collect incident-level crime records over multiple years and connect them to geographic units such as police beats, census tracts, or neighborhoods. I would limit requests to the variables and time periods needed, use pagination and reasonable request intervals when necessary, and cache the raw data locally to avoid repeated requests to the server.
Because web-based data systems can change over time, I would monitor field names, record counts, missing values, date ranges, and sample observations after collection. I would also preserve the original raw data and record the collection date so that changes in the source can be documented and the data-production process can be reproduced.

Chart 1: Variable-Width Column
The 2025 HPI data were summarized by continent. The width of each column represents total population, while the height represents mean HPI across countries within each continent.

hpi_continent <- hpi_2025 %>%
  group_by(Continent) %>%
  summarise(
    population = sum(Population, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_hpi = mean(HPI, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    continent_name = case_when(
      Continent == 1 ~ "Latin America",
      Continent == 2 ~ "N America & Oceania",
      Continent == 3 ~ "Western Europe",
      Continent == 4 ~ "Middle East & N. Africa",
      Continent == 5 ~ "Africa",
      Continent == 6 ~ "South Asia",
      Continent == 7 ~ "Eastern Europe & Central Asia",
      Continent == 8 ~ "East Asia"
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_hpi)) %>%
  mutate(
    xmax = cumsum(population),
    xmin = lag(xmax, default = 0),
    xmid = (xmin + xmax) / 2,
    continent_name = factor(
      continent_name,
      levels = continent_name
    )
  )


ggplot(hpi_continent) +
  geom_rect(
    aes(
      xmin = xmin,
      xmax = xmax,
      ymin = 0,
      ymax = mean_hpi,
      fill = continent_name
    ),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +

  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = xmid,
      y = mean_hpi + 1.2,
      label = sprintf("%.1f", mean_hpi)

    size = 2.6

Some differences may reflect reporting vintages because the World Bank values are from 2024, whereas the Wikipedia table contains country-specific dates ranging from 2024 to 2026. However, the extremely large differences for some countries also suggest differences in source coverage, reporting conventions, or data quality across the Wikipedia entries.


When Is Scraping the Right Tool?
Web scraping is appropriate when the information needed for research is publicly available on a website but is not available through a structured API, downloadable dataset, or other reliable machine-readable source. When an official API or structured dataset exists, it is generally preferable because its schema and data-generation process are more stable and reproducible than scraping a changing webpage.

Therefore, when the necessary variables are available through an API, REST service, or downloadable dataset, I would use those structured sources rather than scrape webpages directly. Web scraping would only be used when relevant public information is available on a webpage but not through a structured alternative.
For a project examining crime patterns and neighborhood change, I would collect incident-level crime records over multiple years and connect them to geographic units such as police beats, census tracts, or neighborhoods. I would limit requests to the variables and time periods needed, use pagination and reasonable request intervals when necessary, and cache the raw data locally to avoid repeated requests to the server.
Because web-based data systems can change over time, I would monitor field names, record counts, missing values, date ranges, and sample observations after collection.
